Zus Health Secures $33M in Series B Funding to Build AI-Powered Clinical Workflows
Global Digital Health News
Story By DHN Bureau
•
9 hours ago
•
3 Mins Read
•
Last Updated On : 13 Nov 2026
The latest funding brings Zus Health's total capital raised to more than $100 million. The company will use the investment to advance its intelligent patient record platform, expand its nationwide healthcare data network and develop AI-powered clinical workflows.
Zus Health, the health technology company founded by Jonathan Bush, has raised $33 million in Series B funding to expand its healthcare data infrastructure and develop AI-powered clinical workflows. The round was led by Drive Capital, with participation from Sanofi Ventures, HealthX Ventures, Alumni Ventures and existing investors Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), F-Prime, Maverick Ventures and JAZZ Venture Partners.
The latest funding brings Zus Health's total capital raised to more than $100 million. The company will use the investment to advance its intelligent patient record platform, expand its nationwide healthcare data network and develop AI-powered clinical workflows.
Founded in 2021, Zus Health has built an API-first, FHIR-native medical record platform designed to consolidate fragmented patient information into a continuously updated longitudinal health record. Its platform connects data from EHR networks, pharmacies, laboratories, care event notifications and other clinical sources, making patient information accessible through APIs, standalone applications, embedded components and direct EHR integrations.
The company's Zus Aggregated Profile (ZAP) combines fragmented clinical information into a unified patient record, supported by AI-powered clinical intelligence. The platform is designed to help healthcare organizations access a more complete view of patients without building their own data connectivity infrastructure.
According to Bush, the company has developed its platform in three layers: a nationwide patient record, a data network that continuously feeds information into the record, and AI-enabled workflows that automate care-related tasks.
"Electronic health record systems (EHRs) succeeded at digitizing healthcare but failed to make patient information portable across organizations," Bush, founder and CEO of Zus Health, told Fierce Healthcare.
The company currently works with value-based care organizations, digital health companies, provider organizations, and diagnostics and precision medicine companies. Its solutions support pre-visit preparation, transitions of care, risk adjustment, quality gap closure and population health management.
Zus reported that its nationwide network supported more than 110 million networked transactions in August, while its AI-native clinical platform generated 39 million evidence citations year-to-date across its solutions.
The company is also seeing growth in specialty care, particularly oncology, where patient records are often distributed across multiple providers. Its aggregated patient data is being used to support treatment eligibility reviews, clinical trial criteria assessments and genetic testing, reducing the manual effort involved in reviewing fragmented records.
"We believe healthcare is entering a new era in which AI can fundamentally change how care is delivered, but that transformation depends on having reliable, connected patient information," said Molly Bonakdarpour, general partner at Drive Capital, in a statement.

articles.title: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding
articles.snippet: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding Fortune
articles.text:
SE3, a Munich-based startup that makes AI software to help drones and other unmanned military systems understand the three-dimensional world around them, has raised $30 million in a Series A round led by Accel.
Recommended Video
Keen, Lakestar, and Seedcamp also participated in the funding round. It comes less than five months after the company, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, emerged from stealth with €5.5 million ($6.1 million) in seed funding.
SE3’s software takes video and sensor feeds from multiple drones and ground vehicles and fuses them into a single 3D picture of the battlefield—”like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game,” cofounder and CEO Lukas Köstler told Fortune .
On top of that map sits a layer that labels objects and how they relate to one another, so soldiers can query it in plain language: How do I reach a target without being seen? What’s a good route for a heavy vehicle?
Operators can also give commands the same way. Rather than remotely piloting a drone with a joystick or having to tap away on a tablet, a soldier can simply say, “I need reconnaissance two kilometers in the north over the forest,” Köstler said, and a suitable drone would take off, fly the mission, and report back.
In addition to this map-level understanding of the battlefield, SE3 also builds the AI systems that sit inside the drones or other unmanned systems, giving them the ability to maneuver and navigate, even in cases where GPS is jammed, detect objects, and act as a “swarm” with other drones.
Köstler, who previously worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research, said the most basic capability—drones locating themselves without GPS—has been delivered thousands of times and is “very robust.”
But he said the high-level fleet command AI is less mature. SE3 has contracts with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, to develop it and has demonstrated it with them, but “there’s still much that needs to be built out over the next one or two years,” he said. The company also has contracts in Ukraine, where its technology is already deployed.
SE3 does not rely on general-purpose, large language models to understand physics or terrain. Instead, it uses classical computer vision algorithms to distill vast amounts of sensor data into a database a language model can query, and gives the model a harness equipped with a variety of conventional software tools the model can call. If the model needs a flight path, a conventional planning algorithm calculates one—avoiding mountains or enemy lines of sight, for example.
Simply feeding raw data to the model “wouldn’t work at all,” Köstler said. Actions such as a drone takeoff can be set to require a human operator’s approval. The system can run entirely offline, and customers can swap in their own preferred frontier AI model to act as the “brains” of the system.
SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), where Köstler and SE3’s CTO, Simon Klenk, were PhD students. Cremers serves as SE3’s chief science officer.
Military work has long made some AI researchers uneasy—a tension highlighted when the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk in March after it refused to let its models be used for fully autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.

articles.text:
Industry

Finite State raises $27 million for device security platform
Finite State has secured $27 million in Series C funding to enhance its AI-driven product security platform. This investment will support global expansion and platform autonomy for connected device manufacturers.
TechGig
Updated On Nov 12, 2026 at 11:40 AM IST
Highlights
Finite State secured $27 million in Series C funding to expand its platform.
The O.H.I.O. Fund led the round with multiple other investors participating.
The platform inspects device software and firmware for vulnerabilities without source code.
It generates SBOMs and VEX documents for compliance with global regulations.
Product security firm Finite State announced on Tuesday that it raised $27 million in a Series C funding round.
The company aims to grow its international presence and make its connected device security platform more autonomous. Private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund led the round, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners.
Advt
The investment addresses two key pressures on manufacturers, according to the company. These include critical flaws like the ‘Vulnpocalypse’ and increasing product security mandates. Finite State’s platform inspects software and firmware in devices, operating from compiled binaries without requiring source code.
It identifies both known and zero-day vulnerabilities, helping manufacturers fix exploitable flaws. On the compliance front, the platform continuously produces SBOMs, VEX documents, and signed compliance packages. This supports device makers in meeting regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 vehicle regulations, and the IEC 62443 industrial standard.
